flags: minor: A, C and D are each contradicted or unsupported (A conflicts directly with paragraph 4; C and D have no support), so B wins by elimination with little real competition
R037-01.notes: Paragraph 5 says noon moved from a fact about the sky to an agreement, and the railroads made that happen. B paraphrases this. A contradicts 'No act of Congress required it'.

R037-02.notes: The sun appears to move westward, and the Boston → New York → Chicago order shows noon coming later the farther west a town is. A town west of Chicago therefore reaches noon later. Needs one short extrapolation; A is the reversal trap.

flags: minor: B, C and D are weak distractors; C contradicts the paragraph's own point
R037-03.notes: The clocks were 'each correct for some line and none correct for the street outside', which shows the confusion from each railroad keeping its own time.

R037-04.notes: Opposing trains 'had to meet and pass at sidings'. C adds a small inference ('set places at set times'). The other choices are unsupported.

flags: minor: the key closely paraphrases the paragraph 3 sentence ('local noon had already passed, clocks were turned back'), so the item is nearly a lookup; B ('set forward') is the only real trap
R037-05.notes: Towns east of the central meridian had already passed local noon. Their clocks were turned back a few minutes, so noon came a second time.

flags: minor: 'missed why the change succeeded' is an inference; the passage never says the objectors failed to see the network's power, only that the railroads 'had something more effective'. It is still clearly the best choice.
minor: A uses the same 'qualified ___' frame with the logic reversed, a good trap for quick readers
R037-06.notes: 'They were, in a sense, correct: the railroads had no legal authority at all. They had something more effective...' The author agrees about the law but points to the real source of the railroads' power. That is qualified agreement.

flags: minor: B and D are implausible; only A ('forceful') works as a trap
R037-07.notes: 'What is striking is who made the change' means it is notable or remarkable.

R037-08.notes: Under standard time, noon is an agreement that no longer depends on the sun. Clocks reading noon before the sun is at its highest shows this. A and D show the old sky-based meaning. C shows the pre-1883 confusion. Applying the idea to a new situation takes a step, and A is tempting because it echoes the shadow line.

flags: minor: overlaps somewhat with R037-06 and R037-01 (all three use paragraph 4's 'no legal authority' point), but each tests a different skill
minor: B, C and D are unsupported and rarely chosen
R037-09.notes: The 1918 date shows that standard time spread by practice (the railroads' schedule, cities following within weeks) 35 years before the law.
